reviews.plausible_gain_reasoning: The guided-cantilever shear stiffness assumes fibres bonded at both ends and the model ignores the soft cover skin, fibre waviness and misalignment from flocking, and viscoelastic barnacle adhesion; about 35 % lower release stress than a commercial topcoat is realistic. The objective gain comes from keeping a compliant layer intact for longer and from macrofouling release after idle periods, about 1 %; slime is unaffected.
key_assumption_issues: Fibres assumed perfectly normal, straight and bonded at primer and skin; flocked fibres are tilted and wavy, changing the shear stiffness by factors
Elastic Kendall energy balance with w = 0.05 J/m^2
Fibre density gradient described in the concept is not modelled
killer_risks: Fibre tips breaking through the thin soft skin create roughness and anchor points for barnacles and weed (as on flock coatings)
Fibre-matrix debonding and fibre buckling under repeated fender loads above ~0.4 MPa
Nylon/PET fibre fragments released when the layer wears (microplastic)

reviews.plausible_gain_reasoning: Thermoresponsive release works in the lab on weakly adhered cells; diatoms consolidate EPS within hours and brush layers age, so a 25 % lower retained slime flux is more realistic than 49 %, giving about 1 % of time-averaged friction. The energy cost is modest, but it is a continuous supply.
key_assumption_issues: Release probability 0.6 per switch and consolidation time 1 day are assumed from lab studies with bacteria, not marine diatom films
LCST switching must stay above the highest route temperature, needing heating to ~45 C
No ageing or fouling of the brush in the model
killer_risks: Embedded heater grid on a steel hull: insulation failure, interference with cathodic protection, fender damage, cabling through the hull
Molecular brush layer ages and is masked by conditioning films
Continuous electrical energy and control system required for the whole service life

reviews.plausible_gain_reasoning: Against an oil-containing foul-release coating an oil-free clay-filled silicone does lose less mobile material, but wear of platelets (not modelled) dominates and the 100 % is by construction; about 60 % lower loss is plausible. The metric says nothing about fouling: clay faces raise surface energy and stiffness, and natural mineral surfaces foul readily, so the objective effect is about zero or slightly negative.
key_assumption_issues: Gain is by construction: the design has no mobile species, so the loss-flux metric cannot fail
Wear, the real loss path of platelets, is not modelled
No model of whether clay faces reduce slime adhesion at all
killer_risks: Clay-faced surfaces are colonised like natural rock; no anti-fouling function
Platelets stiffen the silicone and raise surface energy, worsening barnacle release
Hydration layer in seawater only 1-2 water layers after cation exchange
